Great question & it's one I recently thought to myself but instead of female led I thought gay led since I'm a gay man but we rarely get movies that aren't in some way about social issues. Back to your question though Idk why this is the movie that came to my mind but Spy the Melisa McCarthy & Jason Statham movie is genuinely really funny (which is shocking I know) & any politics or social messages are very much in the background while the humor & action stay up front. I tried to think of a better "Kino" answer to your question but I couldn't think of much that isn't political since art is inherently political.

PAST LIVES and MAY, DECEMBER are 2023 films with female protagonists I really liked. Richard Linklater's Before Trilogy is co-lead and co-written by Julie Delpy. Krzysztof Kieslowski's Three Colours Trilogy and THE DOUBLE LIFE OF VERONIQUE are also great. PERFECT BLUE, GHOST IN THE SHELL (1995), PRINCESS MONONOKE, PATLABOR 2 and ANGEL'S EGG are all excellent anime films with female protagonists.
Some low hanging fruit but AMELIE and PORTRAIT OF A LADY ON FIRE are excellent movies. The latter clearly has some social commentary, but then again ever good movie has something to say

Past Lives was a phenomenal phenomenal movie. Thematically it’s like an adult version of Everything Everywhere All At Once and it’s just such a good movie. Out of every movie I’ve seen this year, I think about this one the most. Just felt like a classic, like early 90’s movie. Beautiful too, such a good movie.

I also want to throw into this as a comedy, Joy Ride was great. It’s a raunchy comedy, obviously not for everyone, but I thought because of its release around Barbie and Oppenheimer, it didn’t get nearly enough love as it should.

Here’s a bunch that I’ve watched recently:

Hereditary - Fantastic film, very creepy, human and stark. Really delves into how grief can completely destroy you. Toni Colette is great in this and does a good job of being somewhat sympathetic but also not that likeable either. Her character has led what seems like a constantly stressed and miserable life, and it shows. 

Midsommar - Same director and same us of a female protagonist, though arguably it does slightly touch on relationships based social issues. But it’s hard a feminist narrative. 

Again it focuses on grief and mourning and the inability to move on. The main character again is sympathetic but hardly a typical protagonist, basically just dissociates at a distance as the plot unfolds. A great metaphor for how many newer generations handle, or rather fail to handle, the more complex and abstract emotions and challenges of life.  Main character has pretty much everything forced upon her, she is largely passive and just existing. 

Suspiria (original) - Amazing arthouse film that is best watched than explained. Another lost girl narrative that forces the female lead to break out of a more helpless mould into a more protagonist like one. 

Don’t bother with the remake though, it is sloppy and ugly. Is more interested in mining the original film for ways to create social and ideological issues. Very little to offer and just made me want to rewatch the original. 

Black Swan - A beatiful psychological thriller that just like Suspiria focuses on the ballet. Obssession, paranoia snd hallucinations make this a dreamlike experience that really leaves you claustrophobic as you forced to experience Nina’s complete breakdown. 

Images - Robert Altman film about a Schizophrenic writer who attempts to live her life as her sanity crumbles. As it’s an early 1970’s film it isn’t the best depiction of mental illness snd can feel exploitative at times. But if you can forgive that it is a hypnotic art house classic. Ending is a bit hokey but the film is gorgeous and surreal enough to make it a non issue. 

A Nightmare on Elm Street - A young Christian girl has to learn about and fight off Freddy Krueger who os killing off her friends. A bit hokey as well and not the greatest acting but otherwise a fantastic horror film that combines more artistic imagery with plain horror. Really lifts the bar on the typical slasher film, there is so much more going on than your average Jason or Michael Myers slash fest.

Is very intelligent in it’s psychological torture of its characters. And Freddy Krueger has a fantastic mix of being genuinely terrifying while also having that dark and uncomfortable sense of humour. 

Nancy is yet another female protagonist who has to slowly earn her stripes. Watching her take on Freddy by the end is truly satisfying. 

Alien/s - this might be a tad controversial but I don’t think Ripley is meant to be a feminist protagonist per se, rather that’s just what she became afterwards. The films really just show her as a somewhat pompous blue collar spacer who ends up way in over her head, but again we see how see rises to the occasion. Then in Aliens we see the long term effects and how she has fallen apart. But ofc she returns to save the day as well as fight her demons.  It is a bit more of a cliche female lead against the world film but it os Alien and Aliens, you can give it a pass. Also because this future universe is so distant and cold to us I liked Ripley’s emotional outbursts and snark, really humanised her. 

Terminator - Sarah Connor again is another example of a female lead who starts of average if a little meek and has to wade through trauma, horror and near death experiences galore. What I like about her in particular is that compared to some of the other films on this list she doesn’t just transition into action hero with ease, in fact she doesn’t really at all. She rises to the occasion in the end but she hasn’t gone through the same old cliche heroic arc. Which sets her up as being completely broken but also bad arse in the second film. She is forced into the occasion and does what she has to, but at a huge price to her sanity and life. 

Neon Demon - tackles the fashion industry in a very unique way. Entire film feels like a surreal fever dream, and all the characters seem like they are usually operating on either forms of upper or downer drugs. 

Main character is an interesting one because she doesn’t have the usual characteristics of a protagonist, and doesn’t really have the arc you would expect. But this is a good thing. 

Though she is also not even that likeable, which I think was on purpose. Anyway it’s an amazing looking film and has a great soundtrack. It is a neon dreamland that transcends into a delirious nightmare. 

So there are so many other films but these were just the ones that sprung to mind. IMO none of these films have heavy social issues or feminist rhetoric guiding the protagonist or film. Though ofc characters like Ripley have ended up as feminist icons anyway.

Steel Magnolias (1989) is the bomb. It's a rare film for so many different reasons. It's not about social issues, it's about family and friendship. It's mostly about a woman and her daughter who has just gotten married. But the daughter has diabetes, if I remember correctly, so she's not supposed to have kids. But then she wants to have kids regardless and that makes her type A mother really upset and there's consequences to her having children. But each woman in the story has her own arc. Like another woman is new to the town (they live in a small town in Louisiana and all have fantastic accents) and she's really skittish because she just got out of an abusive relationship, but you see how she really blossoms in the town because of the friendships that she makes with the other women. Dolly Parton is in and she's a hairdresser in the town and she's married to Sam Shepard and has a grown son but none of the men in her life seem very interested in having much of a relationship with her, which seems really sad because she's Dolly Parton and she's really lively and positive and chatty and everybody loves her. There's more stories too, but I can't remember them all. It's one of those types of movies that you watch and you think, goddamn, that was a fucking good movie (like you really go on a journey with it and a significant enough amount of time passes where you see how people develop and how their lives go through all types of twists and turns, but the friendships and the bonds remain and get them through really tough times). I guess they still make stuff like this, but it seems like it's all multi season TV now, like Big Little Lies or something like that. But what's great about Steel Magnolias is that it's not like 25 hours of content. It's actually really quite remarkable that they're able to do so much in less than 2 hours so it doesn't overstay its welcome. It's a great film that no one talks about anymore, I think because it probably seems dated or hokey. There's also no people of color in it, so it's dated in that way too. It's just a really good story.

Feminine led movies are great and they can show us many sides of femininity.

The social issues and agendas people complain about that I have seen usually come from the eatablisjed franchises or stories that gender swap or dumb down male characters to make the female characters look better.

However I grew up watching Sigourney Weaver take on Xenomorphs and Xena Warrior Princess. Or Dirty Dancing which my interpretation was about a young woman finding herself and her own voice within her social situations and family. The Charlie's Angels movies were great too.

The Long Kiss Goodnight was amazing as well.

The thing for me is in the 80's and 90's men and women could share the lead of a film and their characters stood out. Sure some were typical genre characters but we also had stuff like The Real McCoy with Kim Basinger as a bad ass thief.

To be honest I think overall quality of character and story telling has dropped in the last 15 years. We still get some grms and I want to see strong feminine leads with great stories and movies I want to watch over and over again.

I find this hard, cos so many films that aren’t explicitly *about* feminism are still using a feminist lens. For example *Full Time* is a great film that I recently watched, and the main character kinda ‘just happens’ to be female, but the stresses in her life around being a single mother could land differently if she were a man. The same way, say, *Little Women* is actually concerned with how to live a fulfilling life in a society that has very clear expectations of what women can do, how they should behave, and what their goals should be. *The Babadook* deals with the anxiety of motherhood, as does *Tully*. *The Favourite* wouldn’t make sense if it didn’t contend with gender dynamics to some extent. It’s behind the inciting incident and most everything that comes after in *Thelma and Louise*. The male gaze is a fairly strong sub theme of *The Silence of the Lambs*. You can’t be in *Eighth Grade* without the girl-ness of it all playing a part. *The Florida Project* has the same thing as *Full Time*, in that the underlying struggling single mother thing is a socio-economic reality being indirectly interrogated. *Tar* would hit altogether differently if the lead were male, which is part of what makes it so interesting. 

Off the top of my head, films with female leads that don’t really have anything specifically to do, thematically or sub-thematically, with being female, are:

*Past Lives*

*Arrival*

*When Marnie Was There*

*inside Out*

*A Tale of Two Sisters*

*Howl’s Moving Castle*

*Frances Ha*

*Short Term 12*

*Kiki’s Delivery Service*

*My Life Without Me*

But I’d probably change my mind regarding themes and subthemes if I thought about it some more

Here are a few older ones that I highly recommend

Bridesmaids - Kristin Wiig's comedy which is not only female-led but written and directed! Really funny, moving exploration of female friendships.

  
Terms of Endearment - Phenomenal film starring Shirley MacLaine and Debra Winger as an uptight mother and free-spirited daughter.  
  
Mildred Pierce - Fantastic noir film with lots of atmosphere and great performances. After divorcing her cheating husband, Mildred Pierce (Joan Crawford) must make ends meet to support her two daughters. From her start as a waitress, Mildred builds a successful restaurant franchise. She gives her oldest daughter Veda the best of everything, only to learn all is not what it seems. 

  
All About Eve - Famous Broadway actress Margo Channing (Bette Davis) takes in starstruck Eve Harrington (Ann Baxter) as a protégé, only to be undermined. 

  
Philadelphia Story - The weekend before the society re-marriage of socialite Tracy Lord (Katherine Hepburn), ex-husband (Cary Grant) and two tabloid reporters (Jimmy Stewart and Ruth Hussey) show up, causing a ruckus and a re-think of her life. Funny, highly entertaining, brilliantly written.

   
Born Yesterday - Judy Holliday vehicle about mob boss who goes to Washington with the intent to buy a congressman. While there, he pushes his girlfriend (Holiday) to become better educated so she's not an embarrassment to him and hires tutor William Holden for that task.  As her eyes are opened, she gains confidence in her own value and sees the corruption around her. Holiday is hilarious.

The Descent (2005) - horror film about a group of female cave explorers. All of the (human….) characters with a speaking role are women. It’s a phenomenal work bc they’re a diverse group (mothers, different ages, different countries of origin, age, a poc character, etc) so as a viewer you get to see how they act in the scenario without them having to rely on “types” in the horror genre like the virgin or the hot blonde or the creepy old woman. very enjoyable without being “on the nose” with its messaging

Many classic period drama's fit these criteria. Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, Emma, Wuthering Heights, a lot of these stories have several film adaptations of course. 

Most romantic comedies also don't feature a lot of social commentary.
